--- title: "Linear model" subtitle: "Fit a first-level GLM and check a recovered condition effect." jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: auto --- ## Describe the experiment `fmri_lm(spec, dataset)` fits a first-level model. The specification describes the regressors; the dataset binds observations to timing and events. ::: {#1b840a03 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import fmrimod as fm from fmrimod.spec import hrf from fmrimod.spec import compile as compile_spec from fmrimod.contrast import condition from fmrimod.simulate import simulate_bold events = pd.DataFrame({ "onset": np.arange(6, 198, 8.0), "condition": ["face", "scene", "tool"] * 8, "duration": 2.0, }) spec = hrf("condition", basis="spmg1") ``` ::: We use simulated data with a **known** `face − scene` effect of `2.5` in five of ten voxels, so a correct model must return ≈ `2.5` there and ≈ `0` elsewhere. Compile the specification, resolve the contrast against its column metadata, then generate data with the chosen effect. The normalized coefficient vector makes this exact contrast equal `2.5` without assuming a column position. ::: {#6a4b7aac .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} sampling = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=220, TR=1.0) built, _ = compile_spec(spec, data=events, sampling_frame=sampling) design = np.asarray(built.design_matrix) hypothesis = condition("face", term="condition") - condition( "scene", term="condition" ) placeholder = fm.fmri_dataset( np.zeros((design.shape[0], 1)), tr=1.0, events=events ) weights = hypothesis.resolve( fm.fmri_lm(spec, placeholder).design_columns() )[: design.shape[1]] betas = np.zeros((design.shape[1], 10)) betas[:, :5] = 2.5 * weights[:, None] / (weights @ weights) bold = simulate_bold( design, betas, noise_sd=0.3, n_voxels=10, rng=np.random.default_rng(5), ) dataset = fm.fmri_dataset(bold, tr=1.0, events=events) ``` ::: ## Fit the first-level model `fmri_lm()` compiles the spec into the full event-plus-baseline design and fits it. ::: {#08a8a1d5 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit = fm.fmri_lm(spec, dataset) fit ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` FmriLm( n_coefficients=4, n_voxels=10, residual_df=216.0, config=FmriLmConfig(OLS), contrasts=[], ) ``` ::: ::: `fit.model.design_matrix(run=0)` returns the realized design matrix, including the baseline columns `fmri_lm()` added automatically. ::: {#a7cad0eb .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame( fit.betas, index=list(fit.model.design_matrix(run=0).columns), ).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

Check it alongside a correlation plot: pairwise correlations alone cannot detect every linear dependency. ::: {#670790e6 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} report = fit.condition_report() pd.DataFrame([ {"run": run.run, "columns": run.n_columns, "rank": run.rank, "residual df": run.dfres, "aliased columns": run.aliased_columns} for run in report.runs ]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Compare the fit with the observations For this single-run OLS fit, multiply the realized design by the estimated coefficients to recover the fitted signal. The lower panel shows the observed signal minus that fit. A residual plot can reveal structure the design missed; a visually quiet trace does not establish independent or normally distributed errors. ::: {#11176fd9 .cell fig-height='4.5' fig-width='8' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} X_fitted = fit.model.design_matrix_array(run=0) fitted_signal = X_fitted @ fit.betas observed = dataset.get_all_data() time = np.arange(observed.shape[0]) * 1.0 fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4.5), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]}) axes[0].plot(time, observed[:, 0], color="#aeb8b7", linewidth=1, label="Observed") axes[0].plot(time, fitted_signal[:, 0], color="#24786f", label="Fitted") axes[0].set_ylabel("BOLD signal") axes[0].legend(loc="upper right") axes[1].plot(time, observed[:, 0] - fitted_signal[:, 0], color="#c26143", linewidth=1) axes[1].axhline(0, color="#aeb8b7", linewidth=0.7) axes[1].set(xlabel="Time (s)", ylabel="Residual") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Single-run OLS on simulated data, feature 1. The fitted signal follows the task responses; the residual retains the added noise. This calculation is for the OLS example here, not a general replacement for engine-specific diagnostics.](linear-model_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two panels for the first simulated feature: observed and fitted BOLD signals above, and their residual difference below.'} ::: ::: ## Estimate face minus scene The hypothesis names conditions, not column indices. `fit.contrast(...)` returns a `ContrastResult`, and the estimate comes back at ≈ `2.5` — the value we injected. A model that fit cleanly but applied the contrast to the wrong columns would return a different number here. ::: {#c9c6178c .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} face_vs_scene = fit.contrast( hypothesis, name="face_vs_scene", ) pd.DataFrame({ "estimate": face_vs_scene.estimate.round(3), "t": face_vs_scene.stat.round(2), "p": face_vs_scene.p_value.round(4), }) # voxels 0–4 recover ≈ 2.5; voxels 5–9 are null ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Plot the recovered effect Compare the estimates with the signal used to generate the data. The error bars show uncertainty from this fitted model; they are not a correction for multiple comparisons. ::: {#9b2e9312 .cell fig-height='3.5' fig-width='8' execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5)) feature = np.arange(10) expected = np.r_[np.full(5, 2.5), np.zeros(5)] ax.errorbar(feature - 0.08, face_vs_scene.estimate, yerr=face_vs_scene.se, fmt="o", capsize=3, label="Estimate ± SE") ax.scatter(feature + 0.08, expected, facecolors="none", edgecolors="#c26143", s=50, label="Generating effect", zorder=3) ax.axhline(0, color="#aeb8b7", linewidth=0.7) ax.set(xlabel="Simulated feature", ylabel="Face − scene effect", xticks=feature) ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Simulated effects recovered by the first-level fit. Points show estimates, bars show ±1 standard error, and open markers show the generating contrast effects.](linear-model_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){fig-alt='Estimated face-minus-scene effects for ten simulated features. The first five estimates cluster near 2.5 and the last five near zero, with standard-error bars.'} ::: ::: ## Check the matrix solver `fmri_ols_fit()` solves a design/data pair directly and returns a plain dict of arrays. It skips the spec, the column provenance, and the contrast machinery, so use it only for a bare-matrix cross-check: confirming the high-level fit against textbook OLS, as below. ::: {#afc7b38d .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = np.asarray(fit.model.design_matrix_array(run=0)) matrix_fit = fm.fmri_ols_fit(dataset.get_all_data(), X) # The low-level solver and the typed fit return identical betas. np.allclose(matrix_fit["beta"], fit.betas) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ## Next - [The golden path](golden-path.qmd) — the whole workflow into group, with a parity check - [Contrasts](contrasts.qmd) - [Sketched and AR-aware models](sketched-ar-models.qmd)
